$comment: D-CSUBSET-C11-THREADS-MACHO-MTX-PLAIN-RECURSIVE (and the pe half, D-CSUBSET-C11-THREADS-MTX-PLAIN-RECURSIVE) — the C11 `mtx_recursive` witness on 4 legs. ★★ THE DEFECT IT CATCHES IS A HANG. The macho `mtx_init` recipe passed a NULL mutexattr, and on Darwin a NULL attr is PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT == PTHREAD_MUTEX_NORMAL — non-recursive — so `mtx_init(&m, mtx_plain | mtx_recursive)` returned a mutex its own owner could not re-lock, and the second `mtx_lock` BLOCKED FOREVER. That is invisible to every compile-only pin: the program compiles, links, loads and then stops. ✔MEASURED on the operator's macOS 26.6.2 arm64 host with a C control before the fix: with a NULL attr the same-thread relock did not return inside a 2 s bounded wait; with a RECURSIVE attr it returned at once. The row was filed 2026-07-14 as unobservable because Cycle 1 had no `thrd_create`; P49 landed `thrd_create` on all three formats, which is what made the deadlock reachable and this witness writable. ★★ RECURSION ALONE IS NOT WHAT IS ASSERTED, because an implementation whose mtx_lock were a NO-OP would reach depth 3 happily. The lock COUNT is pinned from a second thread: the worker takes the mutex three times (a non-recursive mutex hangs → exit 12); while it is held main's `mtx_trylock` must report thrd_busy (the lock is real); after TWO of the three unlocks it must STILL report thrd_busy (the count is a count, not a flag — the one assertion an always-recursive fake cannot satisfy); after the third it must SUCCEED. Two of those are the SAME call with OPPOSITE verdicts, so neither a constant thrd_busy nor a constant thrd_success passes this file. ★ AND THE PLAIN CONTROL LIVES INSIDE THE SAME PROGRAM: the `g_gate` handshake mutex is `mtx_plain` and is never re-locked, so honouring `type` breaking the ordinary path fails every handshake rather than an assertion about recursion. `examples/c/c11_threads` is the standing whole-example plain control. ⚠⚠ NOTHING WAITS UNBOUNDED AND NOTHING WAITS ON A CLOCK. Every wait is a bounded poll — at most ~2 s of 2 ms `thrd_sleep` naps, well inside the examples runner's 5 s hang detector — and each timeout has its OWN exit code, so the deadlock this witness aims at reports itself as exit 12 instead of as a killed process. `thrd_sleep` is used because its interval is RELATIVE and monotone-backed on all three platforms: this project's WSL leg has a MEASURED CLOCK_REALTIME that steps ±30 s every few seconds, so no verdict here may be a property of the wall clock, and the stage/go handshake under a plain mutex keeps none of them a property of the scheduler either. ★ THE THREE VEHICLES. elf x86_64 + arm64 (qemu) bind mtx_init/mtx_lock/mtx_trylock DIRECTLY out of libc.so.6 — glibc 2.39 honours mtx_recursive (✔MEASURED through gcc 13.3.0 AND clang 18.1.3, probed separately), so those legs witness the reference behaviour rather than DSS's own. pe64 SYNTHESIZES over kernel32: a CRITICAL_SECTION is always recursion-capable, so the pe arm passed before this cycle too and its job here is to keep doing so. macho SYNTHESIZES over libSystem and is the arm that was BROKEN — it now builds a pthread_mutexattr_t on the stack, sets PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE (2 on Darwin, ✔MEASURED, NOT glibc's 1) when the type carries the mtx_recursive bit, and destroys the attr after init. The kind is MASKED rather than compared, because C11 makes mtx_recursive a bit: `mtx_timed | mtx_recursive` (3) is recursive too, and an equality against 1 would miss it. The 40 + 2 exit code reads two MUTABLE globals so the release arm cannot const-fold it, and a real cross-thread mutex handshake cannot be folded at all. RED-on-disable: delete shippedLibs/threads.json → the #include fires F_ShippedHeaderNotFound and the compile fails; revert the macho recipe to its NULL attr → this example's macho arm times out at exit 12 while `examples/c/c11_threads` stays green.
